St. Seraphim of Sarov

Saints

St. Seraphim of Sarov

Period
1754–1833 (source account)
Region
Russia
Titles / vocation
Monastic
Commemoration
January 2

Introduction

St. Seraphim is remembered as a monk and elder of Sarov. The life begins with his childhood as Prochorus in Kursk and follows his monastic formation, solitary life, and ministry to visitors. It recounts his repose while at prayer in 1833. Accounts of visions, healing, and spiritual counsel remain attributed to the published life rather than newly composed by the app.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

St. Seraphim’s secular name was Prochorus Moshnin. He came from Kursk, where his father was associated with building a cathedral and his widowed mother raised him. He entered Sarov as a young man, later received the monastic name St. Seraphim, and was ordained.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “Prochorus”

Life and notable events

He lived for years in a forest hut near Sarov. The church history reports that robbers severely beat him and later repented after he forgave them. In 1810 he returned to the monastery in obedience to the abbot. In 1825 he opened his enclosure to visitors, later receiving pilgrims at the Near Hermitage.

[2] Ecclesiastical history or testimony · The Orthodox Faith, Church History, Russia: Spiritual Renewal; Seraphim’s solitude and elderhood

Lopukhin’s historical address distinguishes the long preparation in solitude from Seraphim’s later work as an elder receiving people. He describes entry at Sarov in 1778, successive stages of monastic service and seclusion, and finally the opening of his cell to visitors. Lopukhin delivered this interpretation of his life in Belgrade in 1933.

[3] Ecclesiastical history or testimony · Lopukhin, Saint Seraphim and Russia; opening biographical paragraphs

Death and martyrdom

The Sarov account says that he was found kneeling before an icon on January 2, 1833, after smoke was noticed in his cell. His death followed many years after the assault by robbers.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “January 2”

Writings and legacy

He is remembered through disciples, Diveyevo, and writings reporting his conversations, especially the account associated with Motovilov. Motovilov is the named witness to that reported conversation.

[1] Ecclesiastical saint’s life · Published life; biographical narrative, source anchor “Motovilov”

The 1903 synodal act records investigation of reported help associated with Seraphim, examination of his remains, and the arrangements for his glorification. It is the Church’s published record of the decision and its investigation.

[4] Ecclesiastical history or testimony · Act of 29 January 1903; investigation and decision
